content: The HPTN 077 study enrolled both men and women at low risk for HIV infection in Brazil, Malawi, South Africa, and the United States. Similarly, HPTN 084 included participants from these regions. However, neither study specifically targeted populations such as sex workers or people who inject drugs. A small number of transgender men were included in these studies (6 in HPTN 077 and 2 in HPTN 084). All participants in these studies were aged 18 years or older. A meta-analysis of the blinded phases of two efficacy studies demonstrated a 79% reduction in the risk of HIV acquisition among participants receiving long-acting cabotegravir (CAB-LA) compared to those receiving oral PrEP with TDF/FTC. Individually, HPTN 083 estimated a 66% relative reduction in HIV risk with CAB-LA compared to oral PrEP, while HPTN 084 estimated an 88% relative risk reduction. Among the 20 HIV infections identified in the CAB-LA arms of these studies, five were prevalent infections at baseline, seven occurred without recent CAB-LA exposure (either before the first injection or after discontinuation), three occurred during the oral lead-in phase, and five were breakthrough infections during appropriately timed CAB-LA injections. In the safety studies, two seroconversions occurred during the tail phase when CAB levels were below the quantifiable detection threshold. One year of follow-up data from HPTN 083 after unblinding showed similar efficacy results, with 13 new HIV infections in the CAB arm compared to 33 in the TDF/FTC arm. The two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) collectively found a 79% reduction in HIV risk with CAB-LA compared to oral PrEP. Adherence differences likely contributed significantly to the greater efficacy of CAB-LA. In HPTN 084, 98% of incident infections in the TDF/FTC arm were associated with poor or non-adherence. Similarly, in HPTN 083, only two of 39 infections in the TDF/FTC group occurred with drug concentrations consistent with good adherence. Adherence to TDF/FTC was generally lower than adherence to CAB-LA injections. Injection site reactions (ISRs) were common among participants receiving CAB-LA. In HPTN 084, 32% of participants in the CAB-LA arm experienced ISRs compared to 9% in the TDF/FTC arm. Most ISRs were mild, and their frequency decreased over time. In HPTN 077, 38% of participants in the CAB-LA arm reported ISRs compared to 2% in the placebo group. In the ECLAIR study, 93% of participants in the CAB-LA arm reported ISRs compared to 57% in the placebo arm. Despite these reactions, discontinuation due to ISRs was rare, with only 4% of participants in the CAB-LA arm withdrawing from the study. Weight changes and metabolic parameters were also evaluated. In HPTN 084, an initial weight gain was observed among participants randomized to CAB-LA, but no significant differences in mean weight increase were found between the CAB-LA and TDF/FTC arms. Similarly, HPTN 077 found no differences in weight changes or fasting metabolic parameters between study arms. Drug resistance to integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) was analyzed among participants who seroconverted during the studies. Of the 20 infections identified in the CAB-LA arms of HPTN 083 and HPTN 084, seven cases exhibited INSTI resistance mutations, all in HPTN 083. No cases of INSTI resistance were documented in the TDF/FTC arms. Phenotyping results from three cases with INSTI resistance showed varying susceptibility to commonly used integrase inhibitors, with two cases resistant to CAB. Regarding hormonal contraceptive use, a secondary analysis from HPTN 084 found that women on oral contraceptives had lower peak CAB concentrations than those not using hormonal contraception. However, this did not affect other pharmacokinetic parameters. No studies reported on drug-drug interactions between CAB-LA and gender-affirming hormone therapy. Pregnant and breastfeeding women were excluded from participation in both HPTN 077 and HPTN 084. Limited data on pregnancy outcomes were available, with one pregnancy in HPTN 077 resulting in a live birth without birth defects and 49 confirmed pregnancies in HPTN 084, none of which were associated with congenital abnormalities. Behavioral outcomes, including sexual behavior and STI incidence, were not significantly different between study arms. Cost-effectiveness analyses of CAB-LA showed mixed results. Some studies suggested that CAB-LA could be cost-effective or cost-saving when prioritized among certain populations, such as women, or when paired with complementary products like contraceptives. However, in other scenarios, such as among heterosexual men in South Africa, CAB-LA was less likely to achieve cost-effectiveness. Evidence on acceptability and preferences for CAB-LA was derived from a systematic review and qualitative research. There was general interest in injectable PrEP, with preferences for its infrequent dosing and potential to address adherence challenges associated with daily oral PrEP. However, concerns about needle-related fears, injection site pain, logistical challenges, and incomplete protection were reported. Surveys and interviews with PrEP providers showed high levels of support for adding CAB-LA as a PrEP option.
